place.zh: 沂中医 · 一食堂后门 · 夜

setup.zh: 食堂后门的垃圾站，一条叫人踢过的土狗。他蹲下，吸四吐六，等它自己过来。
setup.en: The bins behind the canteen, a stray that has been kicked. He crouches, in four, out six, and waits for it to come.

recap.zh: 吸四吐六收服了红薯；补剂箱里的龙马强力胶囊，一粒一百毫克咖啡因。
recap.en: In four, out six, and Sweet Potato came to him; the Dragon-Horse capsules in the supplement box are a hundred milligrams of caffeine apiece.

zh: 半块烤红薯，搁在手心里。
en: Half a roast sweet potato on his open palm.
"Dogs don't join the team." "How many beats?"

story.zh:
那天晚上，他妈发来一条六十秒的语音，头一句：「芒啊，家长群里那个投篮的，又是你吧？」第二句是他爸，离手机远，嗓门大：「罚球我知道，就是站着投，没人拦你。站着都投不进，下回你坐着投。」后头五十秒，是他妈在骂他爸。

对床的眼镜从一本图书馆的《庄子》后头抬起头，指头点着一行：「『缘督以为经』。督，是脊梁正中那一道。你那第二个，背都弓了。」上铺的老蔡一拍床板：「懂了！背挺直，吐得长——练气入门，先通任督二脉！」眼镜一口气噎在嗓子眼，脸都憋红了，张嘴要骂，想了想，没骂。

九点多，他饿得顶不住，绕到一食堂后门的垃圾站，买了收摊老头最后一个烤红薯。老头朝垃圾桶努努嘴：「留神那个小东西。叫人踢过，谁都不让靠。」

灯影里一条土狗，红黄的毛脏成一绺一绺，脑门正中一撮毛直立着。它压低身子，耳朵往后贴，喉咙里呜呜地响。

沈芒小时候叫邻居家的狗追过三条街。他把红薯往前一伸，「来来来」，那狗往前一蹿，「啪」，牙在他指头前半尺合上了。他往后一跳，跳得比这辈子哪一回起跳都高。

一个怕，一个更怕；一个越怕越凶，一个越凶越怕。下午罚球线上，他也是越怕越憋。

他慢慢侧过身子，蹲下来，眼睛看地。吸，四拍。吐，六拍。一口，两口，三口。心口那阵乱跳慢了下来；那狗喉咙里的声音，也停了。

他掰下大的那一半，搁在摊开的手心里，手背贴地，不往前送，就等。那狗的鼻子先动，眼睛却钉在他脸上，钉了半分钟，才一步一步挪过来，从他手心里叼走了那半块红薯。

他蹲着没动，小小声地喊了一句：

成了！

狗脖子上挂着一个绿牌子：「沂中医动保社　已绝育　已免疫」。「你吃了我半个红薯，你就叫红薯。」他拍一张照片发给阿禾。

「狗不进队。」隔了一会儿，「几拍？」

「吸四，吐六。五口。」

「记了。」

垃圾站的灯底下，一个人蹲着，一条狗趴着，没有一个人看着。没人看着的时候，他行。

院系杯的名单，是对抗赛前一天夜里进的群。针推院队报了十二个人，他是第十二个；中锋是大刘——九月跑去街舞社、叫阿禾一张报名表拉回来的那个一米八八。马小宝回中药学院，站到了对面。

十一月二日早上六点，他一个人在罚球线上吸四吐六。雷老师进门：「罚球前深吸一口，憋住，手才稳。我带了二十年队。」

他把雷老师两根指头按在雷老师自己的腕子上：「您吸四拍……吐六拍。」

吐到一半，雷老师的眉毛动了一下，把手背到了身后：「……接着投。」

六点二十，雷老师往中圈撂下一只纸箱，侧面四个红字：马氏大药房。蛋白粉、肌酸，底下一摞金盒子，一匹红马驮着鹿角：龙马强力胶囊，「人参鹿茸精华 · 增肌三倍」。

马小宝抄起一盒，掂了掂，扔进他怀里：「队友价，零元。三倍。」

「你一回吃几粒？」

「我一粒都不吃。」马小宝摇着摇杯，「那是卖给外人的。我爸说的。」

「那你吃的什么？」

马小宝把摇杯在手心里掂了一掂，没回头：「国外的。NBA都用。」咯吱咯吱，走了。

阿禾的笔尖在本子上停了一下。她把盒子翻到背面，指着那行比蚂蚁还小的字：「咖啡因。一粒顶一杯浓茶。借来的油门，不长肉。」眼镜在场边举着手机：「我查了。《本草》人参那一条，『久服，轻身、延年。』——一个字没讲长肉。」

阿禾伸手到他书包里一抽，带出一张叠着的 A4 纸，昨天她给的「沈芒 · 菜单（两周）」，纸上一圈油印子，正好一个碗口大，洇在「米饭」两个字上。

「泡面碗。」她道，「十月里我问你吃什么，你说食堂。」

沈芒的脸烧了起来。他最怕的就是这一刻。

阿禾却没往本子上写。她把纸叠好塞回去：「下回说实话。没钱，菜单可以改。」

那天夜里，沈芒把金盒子塞进书包最底下，拉上了拉链。那张洇了油的菜单，他铺平了，头一行：「早饭：鸡蛋两个。」离院系杯头一轮，五天。
story.en:
That evening his mom sent a sixty-second voice message. The first sentence: "Mang, the one shooting baskets in the parents' group — that's you again, isn't it?" The second was his dad, far from the phone, loud: "Free throws, I know those — you just stand there and shoot, nobody's stopping you. If you can't make it standing, next time shoot sitting down." The last fifty seconds were his mom telling his dad off.

Specs, on the opposite bed, looked up from behind a library *Zhuangzi* and tapped a line with his finger: "'Follow the du as your constant.' The du is the line right down the middle of the spine. On that second one, your back was hunched." Old Cai slapped the bed board up top: "Got it! Back straight, breathe out long — first step in qi training, open the Ren and Du channels!" Specs choked on his own breath, went red in the face, opened his mouth to tell him off, thought about it, and didn't.

After nine, too hungry to hold out, he went round to the rubbish station behind Canteen One and bought the last roast sweet potato from the old man packing up his stall. The old man jerked his chin at the bins: "Watch out for that little thing. Got kicked. Won't let anyone near."

In the shadow of the light was a mongrel, its reddish-yellow coat matted into dirty clumps, a tuft of hair standing straight up in the middle of its forehead. It crouched low, ears flat back, a whine growling in its throat.

As a boy Shen Mang had been chased three streets by the neighbours' dog. He held the sweet potato out — "Here, here, here" — and the dog lunged; snap, its teeth closed half a foot from his fingers. He jumped back, higher than he had ever jumped in his life.

One was afraid, the other more afraid; the one got fiercer the more afraid it was, the other more afraid the fiercer it got. On the free-throw line that afternoon, he too had held his breath harder the more afraid he was.

Slowly he turned side-on, squatted, eyes on the ground. In, four counts. Out, six counts. One breath, two, three. The wild thumping in his chest slowed down; the sound in the dog's throat stopped too.

He broke off the bigger half and set it in his open palm, back of the hand on the ground, not pushing it forward, just waiting. The dog's nose moved first, but its eyes stayed nailed to his face; they stayed nailed there half a minute before it inched over, step by step, and took the half sweet potato from his palm in its mouth.

He stayed squatting, didn't move, and called out very, very softly:

Done it!

Round the dog's neck hung a green tag: "Yizhong Animal Welfare Society · Neutered · Vaccinated." "You ate half my sweet potato, so you're called Sweet Potato." He took a photo and sent it to Ahe.

"Dogs don't make the team." A while later: "How many counts?"

"In for four, out for six. Five breaths."

"Recorded."

Under the rubbish-station light, a person squatting, a dog lying down, and no one watching. When no one was watching, he could do it.

The roster for the College Cup had come into the group chat the night before the scrimmage. The Acupuncture and Tuina college team entered twelve players, and he was the twelfth; the centre was Big Liu — the six-foot-two who'd run off to the street-dance club in September and been hauled back by Ahe with one sign-up form. Ma Xiaobao went back to the Chinese Pharmacy college and lined up on the other side.

At six in the morning on November the second, he was alone at the free-throw line, in for four, out for six. Coach Lei came in: "Before a free throw, take a deep breath and hold it, that's what steadies your hand. I've coached twenty years."

He pressed two of Coach Lei's fingers onto Coach Lei's own wrist: "You breathe in four counts... out six counts."

Halfway through the breath out, Coach Lei's eyebrows twitched, and he put his hands behind his back: "...Keep shooting."

At six-twenty Coach Lei dumped a cardboard box in the centre circle, four red characters on the side: Ma's Pharmacy. Protein powder, creatine, and at the bottom a stack of gold boxes, a red horse carrying deer antlers: Dragon-Horse Power Capsules, "Ginseng & Deer Antler Essence · Triple Muscle Gain."

Ma Xiaobao picked up a box, weighed it in his hand, and tossed it into his arms: "Teammate price, zero yuan. Triple."

"How many do you take at a time?"

"I don't take a single one." Ma Xiaobao shook his shaker. "Those are for selling to outsiders. My dad said so."

"Then what do you take?"

Ma Xiaobao weighed the shaker in his palm and didn't look back: "Imported. The NBA uses it." Squeak, squeak, and he was gone.

Ahe's pen tip paused on the notebook. She turned the box over and pointed to a line of print smaller than ants: "Caffeine. One capsule, one strong cup of tea. A borrowed accelerator. Builds no muscle." Specs, at the sideline, held up his phone: "I looked it up. In the *Bencao*, the entry on ginseng: 'Taken long, it lightens the body and lengthens the years.' — Not one word about building muscle."

Ahe reached into his backpack and pulled out a folded sheet of A4 — the "Shen Mang · Menu (Two Weeks)" she had given him yesterday. On it was a ring of grease, exactly the size of a bowl's rim, soaked into the word "rice."

"Instant-noodle bowl," she said. "In October I asked what you ate, and you said the canteen."

Shen Mang's face burned. This was the moment he had dreaded most.

But Ahe didn't write it in her notebook. She folded the sheet and slid it back: "Tell the truth next time. No money — the menu can be changed."

That night Shen Mang stuffed the gold box into the very bottom of his backpack and zipped it shut. The grease-stained menu he smoothed out flat; the first line: "Breakfast: two eggs." Five days to the first round of the College Cup.

exits.means: the interlude ends and the story reads on
